---
title: "Write your own character"
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(mascot) # nolint: undesirable_function_linter.
```

"Make your own character" is coming soon to mascot. In version 0.1.0, you can
already read and check a character file using `mascot_read_character()` and
`mascot_check_character()`. Both functions are experimental, and their
arguments, results and diagnostics may change in 0.1.x.

Saving and registering characters and palettes will arrive in 0.1.x. The mascot
studio does not take custom characters yet, but you can preview your own
character offline and use it directly in Shiny apps.

## Find the example character

mascot ships with a sample character recipe, `study_bot.json`. Start by copying
it to a temporary file in `tempdir()` so you can inspect and modify it without
touching package files:

```{r copy-example}
path <- system.file("examples", "characters", "study_bot.json", package = "mascot")
copy <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
file.copy(path, copy)
```

## Read and check the file

Call `mascot_read_character()` with the file path. It reads the JSON file, checks
every field against the character format rules, and returns an opaque, checked
character object:

```{r read-character}
bot <- mascot_read_character(copy)
bot
```

Printing the object shows a concise summary: the character identifier, display
name, family, supported moods, gestures, detail overrides, and the source path.

Checked character objects are self-contained and opaque. Edits to the object
itself are refused at every package boundary. Always edit the source JSON or
plain list, then read or check it again.

## Inside the character format

Opening `study_bot.json` reveals a single JSON object. Every field is verified
against the format rules:

* `format_version`: The integer `1`. This identifies the file grammar.
* `id`: A unique lowercase identifier (`"study_bot"`). Built-in character ids
  (`"tessa"`, `"sela"`, `"knurl"`, `"neer"`) are reserved and refused.
* `name`: The human-readable name shown in titles and summaries (`"Study Bot"`).
* `family`: The character family (`"visorfolk"`). Source recipes can reference a
  family definition for shared default gestures and palettes.
* `requires`: Declared engine capabilities. `study_bot` requires `"parts"`,
  `"outline"`, `"clip"`, `"face_kit"`, `"glow"`, `"tracks"`, and `"lod"`.
  Unsupported and reserved capabilities are refused.
* `colours`: Named colour roles and their default hex values (`body`, `outline`,
  `screen`, `feature`, and `accent`).
* `ground`: Where the character stands: its centre height (`centre_height: 60`).
* `outline`: The width of the outline and the colour role it uses.
* `parts`: The shapes the character is drawn from (in this file `head` and
  `badge_disc`), each with its drawing instructions.
* `anchors`: Named points on parts for attaching accessories or badges.
* `face`: Which part carries the face (`part`), the face `kit` (`"screen"`),
  where it sits (`at`), a `clip`, and the `eyes` and `mouth` settings.
* `moods`: Configurations for the five core moods that every character must
  support: `idle`, `thinking`, `happy`, `worried`, and `celebrating`.
* `gestures`: Named motion tracks. Every character must define moving `wave` and
  `nod` gestures: `wave` must move at least one non-root part (such as a hand or
  antenna), while `nod` may move any channel, including `root`.
* `palettes`: Alternative colour collections (such as `"sea_glass"`).
* `contrast`: Accessibility rules that verify contrast between foreground and
  background colour roles.
* `lod`: Level-of-detail rules for smaller sizes, such as hiding fine details
  like `badge_disc` in the micro detail band.

## Make a small edit

To customise your character, read the JSON into R using `jsonlite`, edit the
fields, and write it back:

```{r edit-character}
data <- jsonlite::read_json(copy)

# Change the identifier and display name
data$id <- "sparky_bot"
data$name <- "Sparky Bot"

# Change the primary body colour from blue to warm coral
data$colours$body <- "#ff6b4a"

# Save the modified JSON back to disk
jsonlite::write_json(data, copy, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE)

# Read and check the edited character
sparky <- mascot_read_character(copy)
sparky
```

`mascot_read_character()` validates the modified file and returns the updated
character object.

## Break it on purpose

The checker stops at the first problem and raises a classed condition of class
`mascot_error_character` (which also inherits from `mascot_error`). The error
carries structured diagnostic metadata:

* `code`: A stable problem identifier (such as `"version"` or `"input_type"`).
* `path`: The JSON path where the error occurred (for example `$.format_version`).
* `value`: The invalid value that was rejected.
* `fix`: Plain-words guidance explaining how to resolve the problem.

Change `format_version` to an unsupported number to see the diagnostic:

```{r break-character}
data$format_version <- 2
jsonlite::write_json(data, copy, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE)

err <- tryCatch(
  mascot_read_character(copy),
  mascot_error_character = function(e) e
)

class(err)
err$code
err$path
err$value
err$fix
conditionMessage(err)
```

The error message clearly states the supported format version:
`"This file is format version 2; this mascot version supports 1. Update the package, or use a version-1 file."`

## Preview and use in an app

Reset the format version to 1 before using the character:

```{r preview-character}
data$format_version <- 1
jsonlite::write_json(data, copy, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE)
sparky <- mascot_read_character(copy)

# Generate an offline comparison preview across moods and sizes
preview <- mascot_preview(character = sparky)
```

Assigning `mascot_preview(character = sparky)` to an object generates an offline
preview page comparing moods, sizes, and light and dark backgrounds without
opening an interactive viewer.

To use your character in a Shiny application, pass the checked object directly to
the `character` argument of `mascot()`. You can also style your character's own
colour roles using `mascot_theme()`:

```{r shiny-usage, eval=FALSE}
library(shiny)
library(mascot) # nolint: undesirable_function_linter.

ui <- fluidPage(
  mascot(
    "helper",
    character = sparky,
    theme = mascot_theme(light = list(screen = "#051b20"))
  )
)
```

`mascot_theme()` checks colour role names against the selected character when
the mascot renders, so custom role names such as `screen` are fully supported.

## What stays the same

The character format is designed with stability in mind:

* **Compatibility promise**: Version-1 character files will keep loading
  throughout the 0.1.x release series.
* **Predictable validation**: The checker only becomes stricter in a new format
  version, except for documented security or resource-safety fixes.
* **Additive features**: New capabilities arrive as new capability names in
  `requires`, leaving existing files untouched.
* **No silent migrations**: Breaking changes will introduce format version 2,
  with the engine accepting both versions. Character files are never modified or
  upgraded silently.

## Coming soon

Upcoming releases in the 0.1.x series will expand support for custom characters:

* **Saving characters**: An export function (`mascot_save_character()`) to write
  self-contained, resolved JSON files with embedded family metadata and face kits.
* **Session registration**: Registering a checked character for the R process
  (`mascot_register_character()`) during application start-up so you can refer to
  it by name.
* **Palette registration**: Registering custom colour palettes across characters.
* **Studio integration**: The mascot studio's **Your character** panel, allowing
  you to upload, inspect and preview custom characters interactively.

```{r cleanup, include=FALSE}
unlink(copy)
```
